beats.lead: The coldest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth was not in the Arctic.
beats.text: Russia's Vostok Station, deep inland on the Antarctic ice sheet, recorded -89.2 degrees Celsius on 21 July 1983, the lowest natural temperature ever confirmed on Earth's surface.
beats.note: This is the coldest figure measured directly. Satellite readings have since detected colder spots elsewhere on the ice sheet.

beats.context: the coldest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth's surface, recorded at Vostok Station on 21 July 1983.

beats.text: Even Vostok's warmest moment on record was brutally cold: -14 degrees Celsius, once, in the middle of the Southern Hemisphere summer.
beats.note: That single reading, on 5 January 1974, is still the warmest this station has ever recorded.

beats.lead: Despite the cold and months of total darkness, Vostok is also one of the sunniest places on Earth.
beats.text: In December it receives an average of about 709 hours of sunshine, nearly 23 hours a day, more than the sunniest spots near the Sahara.
beats.note: It gets zero sunshine at all for roughly four months of the year, May to August, so the sunniest claim is about total hours across the year, not constant daylight.

beats.text: Beneath all that ice sits Lake Vostok, a liquid freshwater lake sealed under about four kilometres of ice for millions of years. Scientists did not physically reach its surface with a drill until 5 February 2012.

beats.line: Earth's cold pole is also, somehow, one of its sunniest places.
